title: The border brief: an ecosystem evidence web
subtitle: Advise a school garden team using relationships and sampling evidence
objective: Describe an ecosystem and biodiversity, then use a food web and sample counts to support a cautious recommendation.

sow.alignment: Directly develops the stated outcome. Original teacher-authored exemplar; route support is responsive and not a qualification or fixed ability label.

priorLearning: Explain that plants make organic substances through photosynthesis.
Read a simple data table and recognise that samples can vary.
success: Distinguish a community from an ecosystem by including abiotic interactions.
Read food-web arrows from food to consumer and predict a possible indirect effect.
Compare species richness fairly without confusing it with total abundance or proof of cause.

vocabulary.meaning: Organisms of one species in a particular area.
Populations of different species living in an area.
A community interacting with the non-living environment.
Living components and effects of organisms, such as predation.
Non-living environmental factors, such as light or moisture.
The variety of life; here we compare species richness as one aspect.
The number of different species present in a stated sample.
The number of individuals present in a stated sample.

equipment: Shared evidence sheet, one selected response route and exit sheet; pencils.
preparation: Read the worked answers and preview the three interactive decisions.
Print shared page 1, one route from pages 2–4, and page 5.
Explain that the food web is a simplified garden model and the counts come from a separate plant-sampling task. They are not measurements of the animals in the web.
safety: The complete route uses printed evidence at desks. No live animals, plants or soil need handling.
Optional follow-up sampling stays within an agreed accessible area; pupils do not taste plants, handle unknown organisms or disturb nests. Wash hands after outdoor work.
practicalAlternative: Use the supplied fictional garden web and matched-area constructed count data. Pupils can make a complete evidence brief within 40 minutes without collecting outdoor samples.

misconceptions.claim: An ecosystem is just a list of animals.
misconceptions.correction: It includes the community, non-living environment and their interactions.
misconceptions.check: Ask where light and soil moisture fit.

misconceptions.claim: Food-web arrows show the predator pointing at its prey.
misconceptions.correction: Arrows show transfer of material and energy from food to consumer.

misconceptions.claim: Twenty organisms always means greater biodiversity than ten.
misconceptions.correction: Abundance alone does not tell us how many species are present.
misconceptions.check: Compare two samples that both contain twenty plants.

misconceptions.claim: One sample proves that a mowing regime caused the difference.
misconceptions.correction: Sampling can vary; other conditions may differ. Repeat comparable sampling and use a fair design before causal claims.
misconceptions.check: Ask what the sample comparison cannot establish.

access.supported: Supply short vocabulary choices, an arrow sentence and counts to circle. Accept a labelled evidence map plus spoken reason.
access.standard: Create a garden brief linking environment, feeding relationships and sample evidence.
access.stretch: Evaluate sampling limits and propose matched repeated measurements to test a maintenance decision. No diversity-index calculation required.
access.regulation: Use a fictional garden decision. Allow quiet written votes and private review. Choose route from retrieval and hinge responses; pupils can change route when appropriate.

slides.title: Which border deserves a closer look?
body: Two garden patches each contain 20 counted plants.
Are they equally rich in species?
A garden team needs an evidence brief.
slides.notes: Introduce a fictional garden decision. More individuals and more species are different claims. Ask pupils to predict what else they need to know before supporting a decision.

slides.title: Build the starting vocabulary
body: R1. What do plants use light for?
R2. Is soil moisture living or non-living?
R3. Does one sample show every organism at a site?
slides.notes: R1 photosynthesis. R2 non-living. R3 no; a sample represents part of a site and may miss species. Revisit sample versus population if needed.

slides.title: I explain an interaction
body: A community includes populations of different species.
An ecosystem includes their environment and interactions.
I connect an abiotic factor to a living response.
slides.notes: Think aloud: light is abiotic. Its availability can affect plant photosynthesis. Plant cover can change shade and moisture conditions. An ecosystem explanation includes relationships, not just two disconnected lists. Soil contains living and non-living components; soil moisture is the non-living factor here.

visual.title: An ecosystem includes interactions
visual.description: The community panel names organisms. The abiotic panel names light, temperature and soil moisture. Directed labelled links show that light supports plant photosynthesis and plant cover can affect shade and soil moisture.

elements.text: More than a list of living things

Plants
Aphids and caterpillars
Ladybirds and blue tits

slides.title: I read the arrow in the right direction
body: Leaf → aphid means the aphid feeds on the plant.
Arrows show food-to-consumer transfer.
A web joins several feeding routes.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Trace leaves → aphids → ladybirds and leaves → caterpillars → blue tits. The model selects plausible garden feeding links and omits decomposers and other foods. It does not predict exact population sizes or timings.

visual.title: A selected garden food web
visual.description: Plant leaves feed caterpillars and aphids; blue tits eat caterpillars and aphids; ladybirds eat aphids. Arrows run from the food to the consumer. Decomposers and many additional links are omitted.

elements.text: Selected garden feeding links; arrows carry energy and material.

slides.title: I count species separately from individuals
body: Abundance counts individuals.
Richness counts the different species present.
Equal sample totals can have different richness.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Work the analogous mini-example aloud: sample X contains 3 daisies and 3 clover plants, so 6 individuals and 2 species. For the displayed main data ask pupils to do their own counting during We do. A zero means not recorded in this sample, not proven absent everywhere.

visual.title: Plant sample counts
visual.description: Constructed equal-area samples contain twenty individuals each. Patch A has sixteen daisies and four clover plants, with zero dandelions or plantains. Patch B has five individuals of each of the four named species. Counts are not whole-site totals.

elements.text: Equal totals can hide different richness

Constructed data: one 1 m² sample per patch.
Bar length shows number of individual plants; totals = 20 each.

slides.title: The garden evidence desk
body: W1. Use card A to explain an ecosystem interaction.
W2. Trace a possible effect of fewer aphids.
W3. Compare counts without overclaiming.
slides.notes: 8 minutes across three We do steps. First classify soil moisture as abiotic and aphid feeding as biotic, then connect one factor to an organism. All necessary web links and counts are printed on shared page 1.

table.caption: Constructed data: one 1 m² sample in each patch. Counts are individual plants.

slides.title: Predict a possible knock-on effect
body: Aphid abundance falls.
What could happen to ladybirds, and why?
Why is the outcome not guaranteed?
slides.notes: W2: ladybirds may have less prey and their abundance may fall, but alternative foods, movement, timing and other factors could alter outcomes. Blue tits also have other foods in the simplified web. Do not use numerical reductions or inevitable extinction.

slides.title: Write a claim the evidence can carry
body: Both samples contain 20 individuals.
Which has greater recorded richness?
Does this prove a maintenance method caused it?
slides.notes: W3 A=2 recorded species, B=4, so B greater recorded richness in these samples. Totals equal. Cannot establish site-wide biodiversity or cause from one sample per patch. Teacher helps replace “proves” with “in these samples”.
slides.reveal: Patch B: 4 recorded species. Patch A: 2. One sample cannot establish the cause.

slides.title: Choose the defensible headline
body: Which headline matches our data?
slides.notes: A incorrect: abundance and richness differ. B correct, bounded by the samples. C incorrect: one sample and no controlled comparison cannot prove cause. If uncertain, count non-zero species separately from summing individuals.

options.text: Both patches have identical biodiversity because totals match.
options.feedback: Equal abundance does not imply equal richness or all other biodiversity measures.

options.text: Patch B has greater recorded species richness in these samples.
options.feedback: Four species were recorded in B compared with two in A.

options.text: The mowing method definitely caused the difference.
options.feedback: The data do not isolate mowing or rule out sampling variation.

slides.title: Write the garden team’s brief
body: Choose one response route.
Explain an interaction and a feeding relationship.
Use a numerical comparison and a limit.
slides.notes: 10 minutes independent. Core evidence is an ecosystem relationship, correctly directed feeding link, and bounded richness comparison. Pupils may draw with labels or dictate their own analysis. A recommendation is to investigate further, not to claim a proved cause.

slides.title: Check your arrows
body: Can you read each arrow as “is eaten by”?
Does a consumer have another food in the model?
Use “may” when explaining a population change.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Prompt checking without correcting individual arrows before they attempt the task.

slides.title: Check your evidence language
body: State what was counted and the sample area.
Separate number of species from total individuals.
Name one next measurement you would make.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Repeated matched-area plant samples at randomly selected locations are an appropriate next step. Measuring another relevant factor can help interpret differences.

slides.title: Peer-review the brief
body: Underline the relationship, numerical evidence and limit.
Find one claim that is too strong.
Revise it after feedback.
slides.notes: Offer teacher or private self-review as alternatives to peer review. Accept distinct accurate abiotic links. Do not penalise pupils for choosing a cautious recommendation.

slides.title: Give the garden team a question
body: Choose one next question about the patches.
Explain which evidence would answer it.
We will select a question for later sampling.
slides.notes: Lundy: capture pupils’ questions, choose one feasible follow-up and explicitly report how their reasoning influenced the next task. Do not require pupils to promise outdoor participation.

slides.title: Make three ideas precise
body: E1. What makes an ecosystem more than a community?
E2. What does a food-web arrow show?
E3. Can total abundance alone tell us richness?
slides.notes: E1 interactions with abiotic environment. E2 transfer from food to consumer. E3 no; need counts split by species. E4 pupil sheet asks one sampling improvement. Collect before model answer.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: garden brief
pupilPages.intro: Fictional garden model. Plant counts below are constructed data from one 1 m² sample per patch.

blocks.text: A • Environment: soil moisture and light can affect plants. Aphids feed on plants; ladybirds feed on aphids. B • Selected food links: leaves → caterpillars; leaves → aphids; aphids → ladybirds; caterpillars → blue tits; aphids → blue tits. Arrows run from food to consumer.

blocks.prompt: W1. Name an abiotic factor and explain one interaction with a living organism.
W2. Fewer aphids: predict one possible ladybird effect and say why it is uncertain.
W3. Compare abundance and richness. Can these samples prove the cause?

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: a clear garden message
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Word bank: non-living / consumer / two / four / twenty.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which is an abiotic factor?
S2. Complete: An ecosystem includes living organisms interacting with each other and the ____ environment.
S3. Draw leaves → aphids → ladybirds. Explain what one arrow means.
S4. Complete: A has ____ species and B has ____ . Each sample contains ____ individual plants.
S5. Give one reason to take more samples before making a site-wide claim.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: a garden brief
pupilPages.intro: Use the evidence sheet. Each answer should help the team make a careful decision.

blocks.prompt: N1. Describe one abiotic interaction and one biotic interaction in the garden.
N2. Draw two connected food chains from the model. Predict a possible effect of fewer aphids and explain one uncertainty.
N3. Compare abundance and species richness using values for both samples.
N4. Recommend a next sampling step and explain why the current data cannot prove a maintenance cause.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: challenge the headline
pupilPages.intro: Claim: “Patch B’s mowing method has doubled the biodiversity of the whole garden.” The evidence is only the one sample per patch on page 1.

blocks.prompt: T1. Identify two different overclaims and rewrite the headline so that it matches the evidence.
T2. Propose a comparison using repeated equal-area plant samples. Explain how you would select locations and keep effort comparable.
T3. The team wants to remove all aphids. Use the web to explain two possible effects and one limitation of the model.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Work independently. A labelled diagram or scribed answer is welcome.

blocks.prompt: E1. What must an ecosystem description include beyond the community?
E2. What does the arrow aphid → ladybird show?
E3. Why can two samples with equal total abundance have different species richness?
E4. Name one improvement to the sampling and explain its purpose.
Reflection. Which question should the garden team investigate next, and why?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1 photosynthesis. R2 soil moisture is non-living/abiotic. R3 one sample is incomplete and may miss organisms or species.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 e.g. soil moisture affects plant growth, or light affects photosynthesis; aphid feeding is biotic. W2 fewer aphids may reduce food for ladybirds and lead to fewer ladybirds, but alternative prey, movement or other factors can affect the outcome. W3 both have 20 individuals; A records 2 species and B 4. B has greater recorded richness in these samples. These data do not prove a cause or full-site biodiversity.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A wrong: equal abundance does not mean equal richness. B correct and limited to the evidence. C wrong: sampling variation and confounding factors are unresolved.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 soil moisture. S2 non-living. S3 correct arrow sequence; leaves are eaten by aphids, aphids by ladybirds, transferring material and energy. S4 two/four/twenty. S5 samples vary and one small area may miss species; more comparable samples improve the estimate.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1 abiotic: light→photosynthesis or soil moisture→plant growth; biotic: feeding or a justified competition example. N2 e.g. leaves → aphids → ladybirds and leaves → caterpillars → blue tits. Fewer aphids may reduce ladybird food; other prey/movement/interactions create uncertainty. N3 abundance 20 both; richness A 2 / B 4. N4 repeat equal-area samples at randomly selected locations in both patches using comparable identification and effort; one unmatched observational comparison does not isolate maintenance from other factors.

answers.label: T1–T3
answers.answer: T1 the count measures recorded plant richness in small samples, not all biodiversity in the whole garden; causal attribution to mowing is unsupported. Accurate rewrite: “Our equal-area sample from B recorded four plant species, compared with two in A; further sampling is needed.” T2 sample several randomly selected equal-area quadrats in each defined patch, at comparable times with the same counting/identification rules and equal effort; record relevant conditions. To test mowing causally, use replicated comparable plots with assigned regimes and before/after measurements where feasible. T3 aphid feeding damage may fall; ladybirds may lose prey; blue tits could lose aphids as prey but have other food. The web omits many foods, movements, abundance and timings, so exact size or certainty cannot be inferred.

answers.label: E1–E4 / reflection
answers.answer: E1 abiotic environment and interactions with living organisms. E2 ladybird consumes aphid; transfer from food to consumer. E3 individuals can be distributed among different numbers of species. E4 repeated randomly located equal-area samples reduce selection bias and show variation; common method/equal effort improve comparability. Reflection accepts a relevant evidence-seeking question and reason.

answers.label: Evidence and responsive teaching
answers.answer: Secure core: explains an ecosystem interaction, reads food-to-consumer arrows, and gives A 2 / B 4 richness while recognising abundance 20 each and a sampling limit. Re-teach reversed arrows with “is eaten by”; re-teach richness confusion by counting only rows with non-zero values before adding individual counts. Formal diversity indices, trophic efficiency and population equations are not required.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Print shared page 1, ONE selected response route (2, 3 or 4), and exit page 5. Do not require all routes. Adult scribing records the pupil’s own words.
This is an introductory Topic 9 lesson after the planned Topics 7–8 assessment. Later lessons can develop quadrats, transects, abundance estimates and biodiversity measures.
The selected food web and the separate plant dataset serve different reasoning tasks. Do not imply the plant counts measured the animals in the web.

No real school biodiversity claim is made. The constructed data intentionally keep total abundance equal to isolate the richness distinction. Zero means not recorded in that sample, not certain absence at the site.

Teacher vocabulary extension: biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem variation; species richness is one useful but incomplete measure. Greater richness alone does not establish a healthier site in every ecological context.

interactive.title: The garden decision desk
interactive.intro: Choose a prediction, test the diagram, then explain. Pause or reset at any time. Paper W1–W3 use the same evidence.
